@@82742928 <h> Six Tax-Based Ways to Tackle US Inequality <p> Some of the leading candidates for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination have proposed radical measures to reduce inequality , such as a wealth tax . But there are many other progressive tax policies that would be both easier to enforce and more likely to get a Democratic candidate elected . <p> CAMBRIDGE -- Three years ago , Donald Trump 's victory in the United States ' presidential election triggered a search for explanations of what is still a shocking outcome . One immediately came to dominate : his Democratic opponents had been insufficiently aware of the problem of income inequality , or had neglected to propose effective solutions . <p> That is presumably the logic behind the radical proposals to tackle inequality coming from some of the leading candidates for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination . Senator Elizabeth Warren , for example , has proposed an annual tax ( originally of 2% , but now up to 6% ) on the richest Americans ' wealth . <p> The problem with the wealth tax is not that it is radical . Like many economists , I would support a high carbon tax -- also a radical policy , but the most economically efficient way to respond to the global problem of climate change . A wealth tax , however , simply is not the most efficient way to address the problem of inequality . <p> In fact , there are at least six practical policy changes that could make the US tax system more progressive . They have all been proposed by mainstream Democrats such as President Barack Obama -- who also advanced the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and other inequality-reducing policies -- but in most cases were blocked by Republicans . <p> These proposals are practical in two senses . For starters , if adopted , they would be more enforceable than a wealth tax and less likely to have costly unintended side effects . Moreover , studies of recent US congressional elections have found that the traditional median-voter approach still holds . Although radical-left economic proposals do attract new voters on the left , they repel substantially more voters on the right . That suggests US political candidates are more likely to get elected by proposing moderate policies than by advocating radical measures . <p> The first policy proposal would be to reinforce the estate tax . The US might begin by restoring the tax on all estates worth , say , $5 million . More important , however , is to eliminate the " step-up " of the valuation of the assets in the estate , which currently allows generations to pass on capital gains without ever paying tax on them . It would be far easier for the Internal Revenue Service to place a dollar value on assets on a once-a-lifetime basis ( that is , on the estate , before it passes to the heirs ) than to try to do so every year under a wealth tax . And doing this would accomplish the same objective as the wealth tax : putting some friction into the inter-generational accumulation of dynastic wealth that , as it stands , never gets taxed . <h> Subscribe now <h> Subscribe today and get unlimited access to OnPoint , the Big Picture , the PS archive of more than 14,000 commentaries , and our annual magazine , for less than $2 a week . <p> SUBSCRIBE <p> Second , policymakers should give the IRS the resources it needs to collect taxes that are owed . Natasha Sarin and Larry Summers recently noted that the IRS currently fails to collect nearly 15% of total tax liabilities -- primarily to the benefit of those with high incomes . It is impossible to close the gap completely . But giving the IRS more resources , Sarin and Summers argue , would have a high benefit-cost ratio and generate more than $1 trillion in net additional revenue over the next decade . <p> Third , expanding the Earned Income Tax Credit ( EITC ) would help to " make work pay . " Incentives do matter . But it is those Americans trying to lift themselves out of poverty and up into the middle class -- not the rich -- who often face the steepest effective marginal tax rate ( taking lost benefits into account ) . Extending the EITC to more households would enlarge the economic pie while also sharing it more equally , thereby enhancing both efficiency and equity . <p> Fourth , the payroll tax should be made more progressive . The US social-security system is not as progressive as many think . Even workers who do n't earn enough to pay federal income tax must nonetheless pay a payroll tax . The threshold for this tax should be raised , with the lost revenue recouped by raising the ceiling ( currently $118,500 in wages ) above which Americans no longer pay it . <p> Fifth , the US government also should make the income tax more progressive -- for example , by cutting the gap between the tax rates on investment income and wages . And , clearly , it should abolish the carried-interest loophole . <p> Finally , Congress should revisit the December 2017 corporate-tax cut to make it revenue-neutral . There were good arguments for reducing the US corporate-tax rate to bring it closer to that of other countries . But all Republican senators voted for the tax cut in the declared belief that it would boost income growth so much as to be revenue-neutral . Unsurprisingly , this has not happened : firms turned their windfalls over to shareholders in the form of dividends and share buy-backs , rather than investing in capital as intended . As a result , revenue fell . US firms now pay virtually the lowest level of tax as a percentage of GDP among major advancedeconomies . <p> The solution is not to limit firms from buying back their shares , as Senators Bernie Sanders ( another leading Democratic presidential contender ) and Chuck Schumer have proposed . Rather , the key is to close loopholes in order to bring overall corporate-tax revenue back to its pre-reform level . The biggest potential revenue-generator is to curtail the tax-deductibility of interest payments -- another proposal that could be good for both GDP and income distribution . If there is to be a successor to the 2007-2009 financial crisis , it is now more likely to come from an excess of corporate debt -- especially of the so-called " covenant-lite " variety -- than from too much housing debt . Curtailing the interest-rate deduction could motivate firms to strengthen their financing structure . <p> Fortunately , few of the Democratic presidential candidates have committed themselves irrevocably to extreme policies . It is not too late for Warren or others to adopt further proposals to address inequality that are more practical than the wealth tax and would naturally precede it . <p> Jeffrey Frankel , Professor of Capital Formation and Growth at Harvard University , previously served as a member of President Bill Clinton 's Council of Economic Advisers . He is a research associate at the US National Bureau of Economic Research , where he is a member of the Business Cycle Dating Committee , the official US arbiter of recession and recovery . <p> " economically efficient " is a slippery concept , all the more so when big money is on the line ... <p> I think much of the push for wealth tax comes from the fact that today 's rich individuals ( and corps , if applicable ) pay only a fraction of even the historically low income tax rate we have now . To make it worse , most of Congress on both sides of the aisle seems pretty much content with that . <p> All six are good proposals , but as additions to rather than substitutes for a wealth tax . A wealth tax should n't be the only tool for addressing inequality , but establishing a public data base on wealth and public claims in regard to wealth are too important to be neglected entirely . <p> How about the massive Federal expense savings that could be achieved if efficiency standards were adopted by all branches of goverment the way private business operates . But then as you reduce Government Employees by efficiency you also loose control over their vote , I suspect Politicians find it easier to leverage their vote for campaign donations by proposing Tax Schemes ( always against deep pocketed entities ) proposed to help society , but often do the opposite . <h> New Comment <p> It appears that you have not yet updated your first and last name . @@82749231 <p> Thank you for visiting nature.com . You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS . In the meantime , to ensure continued support , we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript . <h> Subjects <h> Abstract <p> A central issue in ecology is understanding how complex and biodiverse food webs persist in the face of disturbance , and which structural properties affect disturbance propagation among species . However , our comprehension of assemblage mechanisms and disturbance propagation in food webs is limited by the multitude of stressors affecting ecosystems , impairing ecosystem management . By analysing directional food web components connecting species along food chains , we show that increasing species richness and constant feeding linkage density promote the establishment of predictable food web structures , in which the proportion of species co-present in one or more food chains is lower than what would be expected by chance . This reduces the intrinsic vulnerability of real food webs to disturbance propagation in comparison to random webs , and suggests that biodiversity conservation efforts should also increase the potential of ecological communities to buffer top-down and bottom-up disturbance in ecosystems . The food web patterns observed here have not been noticed before , and could also be explored in non-natural networks . <h> Introduction <p> The complexity of food webs and the multitude of stressors affecting ecosystems limit our comprehension of how disturbance propagates in ecological communities , hampering biodiversity conservation and management . To cope with such complexity , ecologists have investigated the relationship between the topology of food webs and their stability1 , seeking to understand whether and how the number of species underlies biodiversity architecture and stability to perturbation2 . May3 argued that in randomly assembled multispecies systems , increasing species richness reduced system stability . This prompted several subsequent studies , which established that the arrangement of food webs with respect to the number of species they contain is not random4,5,6 , and that such non-random structures are more stable to perturbation than what is expected by chance7,8,9,10 . Recently , studies have focused on network-level properties of food webs that promote community persistence9,11 , resilience to perturbations10 and resistance to species loss12,13,14 . Nevertheless , our understanding of disturbance propagation mechanisms in real ecosystems is still limited . In addition , while food web modelling has fundamentally advanced our understanding of their structure and dynamics , the complexity of the phenomena , the quantity of data involved and the computational skills required have limited the ability to translate such science-based knowledge into practical advice supporting policy formulation15,16 . Such insight is particularly urgent in a scenario of global change , given the evidence suggesting that both anthropogenic pressure and climate change have the potential to disrupt top-down and bottom-up control mechanisms that regulate ecological **25;56;TOOLONG , highlighting the need for management strategies aimed at preserving stable food webs in ecosystems22,23 . <p> Within food webs , disturbance can propagate along food chains either from a basal resource towards its consumers and their predators ( bottom-up pathway ) or from a predator to its prey and their resources ( top-down pathway ) . In directional terms , such pathways can be grouped into sink or source sub-webs , which include all the food chains originating from or converging to a single basal or top species respectively24 . By propagating through feeding links , even small changes in species ' traits and single extinction or invasion events can significantly impact ecological communities13,25 . Nevertheless , despite the importance of top-down and bottom-up controls on the dynamics of populations and ecological processes19,20,24,26 , the mechanisms determining the distribution of species in sink and source sub-webs , as well as the relationship between species richness and the proportion of species sharing food chains in real food webs , have yet to be fully explored . <p> We investigated the relationships between species richness , food web complexity and the distribution of species into source and sink sub-webs . We also considered a third type , the cross sub-web , which involves disturbance propagating in both directions from an intermediate species ( Fig. 1 ) . These represent fundamental aspects of biodiversity organisation , and underlie the potential of disturbance to propagate across trophic levels13,24,25,27,28 . Accordingly , we assumed that the higher the proportion of species co-present in at least one food chain within a food web , the higher the potential of disturbance to propagate13 . The intrinsic vulnerability of food webs to the propagation of disturbance along food chains was thus quantified as the proportion of species ( P ) included in each source ( PB ) , cross ( PC ) and sink ( PT ) sub-web , originating from each basal , intermediate or top species respectively . Here , we focused on detritus-based food webs . The detritus compartment plays a fundamental role in ecosystem structure and functioning29,30 , and climate change is expected to affect detritus inputs and organic matter decomposition rates in ecosystems31,32 . Nevertheless , very little information that might help to understand the structure of these donor-controlled systems is available . <p> Figure 1 <p> Panel ( a ) Comparison of three simple networks containing the same number of species ( nodes ) and trophic links ( lines ) . In network 1 , all species are part of one food chain , and a disturbance originating from any given species would directly propagate along the food chain to all the remaining ones . In network 2 , a bottom-up disturbance spreading from species 1 would affect species 4-5-6 only . In network 3 , the modification of a single link with respect to network 2 would mean that only species 4 would be directly affected by a bottom-up disturbance propagating from species 1 . Panels ( b -- d ) Food sub-webs exemplifying various propagation pathways along food chains for disturbance starting from a single species ( circled ) : ( b ) bottom-up propagation from a basal resource ( red ) , ( c ) cross propagation from a primary consumer ( orange ) , and ( d ) top-down propagation from a predator ( yellow ) . <p> We compared food webs belonging to both aquatic and terrestrial habitats in the Mediterranean region ( Table 1 ) , and we quantified their vulnerability to disturbance propagating from species on various trophic levels . We then sought to verify whether the observed PB , PC and PT values were ( i ) dependent on species richness ( S ) and web connectance ( Cmin ) and ( ii ) predictable using a mechanistic food web model6 or similar to what would be expected by chance . This was achieved by comparing field data with random food web models , as well as webs generated using the niche model6 , a simple yet predictive food web model based on observed S and Cmin values and a few foraging rules constraining the probability of feeding interaction between species . The comparison of observed and random food web structures can provide important insight into the organisation of ecological communities . Indeed , the association of food web stability with non-random structures enhances our understanding of the ecological factors constraining the observed patterns and hence the mechanisms underlying the emergence and persistence of complex food webs7 . <p> Table 1 Food webs representative of various habitats in the Mediterranean region . Locality indicates the region , country and GPS coordinates for each habitat . <h> Results <h> Species richness and food sub-webs <p> Food web connectance ( Cmin ) varied from 0.073 in Stream to 0.130 in Lake ( Table 1 ) , decreasing with species richness ( S ) ( Fig. 2 ) . On average , bottom-up propagation pathways ( PB ) included a higher proportion of species than cross ( PC ) and top-down ( PT ) propagation pathways ( Fig. 3 ; one-way ANOVA for repeated measures : F ? = ? 36.7 , p ? &lt; ? 0.0001 ; associated Tukey 's pairwise comparisons : Q always ? &gt; ? 4.4 , p always ? &lt; ? 0.01 ) . In contrast , PB , PC and PT were not related to the proportion of basal or top species ( p always ? &gt; ? 0.05 ) . No differences in the correlation slopes between PB , PC and PT and either S or %I were observed ( ANCOVA and the homogeneity of slopes test , F ? &lt; ? 1 and p ? &gt; ? 0.05 in both cases ) . In contrast , the correlation slope between PB and Cmin was lower than what was observed for PC and PT ( ANCOVA and homogeneity of slopes test , F ? = ? 4.5 and p ? = ? 0.01 ) . <p> Figure 2 <p> Panels ( a , b ) relationship between species richness ( S ) , number of feeding links ( L ) and food web connectance ( Cmin ) observed in our dataset ( red symbols ) and estimated from the link-species scaling law ( black symbols ) and the constant connectance hypothesis ( empty symbols ) . As a consequence , the observed PB , PC and PT values were similar to those expected on the basis of the LSSL ( Fig. 2c ) , while they were significantly lower than what would be expected on the basis of the constant connectance hypothesis34 ( CCH ) ( Two-way ANOVA and Tukey 's pairwise comparisons , p ? &lt; ? 0.05 ) , which predicts that L/S will increase with S , L will increase as L ? = ? 0.2S2 and Cmin will not vary with S ( Fig. 2c ) . Lastly , starting from the observed S and Cmin values , we generated model food webs based on the niche model6 , which were then compared with random food web models . The niche model-generated webs closely predicted the mean and habitat-specific PB , PC , PT and V values observed in the real food webs ( Fig. 2d-h ) . In contrast , the random model-generated webs were characterised by markedly higher values ( Fig. 2d , one-way ANOVA for repeated measures and Tukey 's pairwise comparisons , p always ? &lt; ? 0.05 ) . <h> Discussion <p> The distribution of species across source , cross and sink sub-webs differed between habitats in a predictable way in accordance with food web size ( S ) and connectance ( Cmin ) . The higher the number of species , the lower the proportion of them co-present in at least one food chain . This indicates that the vulnerability of ecosystems to disturbance propagation across trophic levels falls as their species richness rises , which implies that more biodiverse communities are potentially more able to buffer disturbance . Our observations are also consistent with recent results from studies based on model food webs of similar species richness13 , where higher connectance intensified the effect ( i.e. caused a higher rate of secondary species loss ) of single perturbation events ( i.e. successful species invasions ) . As well as species richness , a high number of intermediate species relative to the total reduced the potential of disturbance to propagate along food chains . In addition , our data satisfied expectations from the link-species scaling law , which predicts constant linkage density among species . According to foraging optimisation theories , ( i ) a low and roughly constant linkage density between species arises from the selection by consumers of the lowest number of food items that maximises their net energy intake9,35 , and ( ii ) prey species richness promotes predator trophic specialisation , as shown in the food webs analysed here32,36 and elsewhere9,37 . This suggests that energetic constrains on foraging strategies , which operate at the individual level38 , may give rise to food webs which are intrinsically less vulnerable to the propagation of disturbance than what would be expected if consumers tended to generalise as the number of their potential food sources increased39 . Notably , the random food web models failed to reproduce real patterns , while niche model-generated webs closely predicted the observed values . Our results thus imply that the distribution of species in source , cross and sink sub-webs significantly deviates from random , and that the patterns observed in real food webs benefit ecological communities by reducing vulnerability to disturbance propagation along food chains compared to what would be expected if distribution was determined by chance . <p> Regardless of habitat type , source sub-webs included a higher proportion of total species than cross and sink sub-webs . This implies that disturbance propagating from a basal resource would have a significantly higher potential to spread throughout the food web than disturbance propagating from a top or an intermediate species . We speculate that the observed patterns may promote stability in detritus-based systems , where the availability of basal resources ( i.e. organic detritus and colonising microfungi ) is expected to be much more stable over time than invertebrate populations , often characterised by marked spatial-temporal variations and sensitivity to stress40,41 ( see Fig . S2 for supporting results ) . On the other hand , global change is expected to affect the dynamics of the detritus compartment in ecosystems31,32,42,43 . Thus , our data suggest that there is a strong likelihood of future environmental changes in Mediterranean ecosystems giving rise to bottom-up effects mediated by the structure of detritus-based food webs . <p> The coefficient of variation of Pi values increased with the number of species within each food web , and it was inversely related to food web vulnerability to disturbance . Together with the PB , PC , PT and V values , this makes the variation of species ' Pi values within a food web a useful a-priori indication of its vulnerability . We acknowledge that our observations are based on static food web structures , and that the reorganisation of trophic links and/or changes in linkage strength between species in accordance with their trophic niche plasticity could modify the effects of disturbance25 . Nevertheless , our analysis of sub-webs enabled us to evaluate the intrinsic vulnerability of real food webs to a range of disturbance propagation pathways ( i.e. bottom-up , cross , and top-down ) . This approach is expected to yield information useful to management strategies based on the risk of ecosystem-specific disturbance propagation , regardless of food web compilation methods . Analysis of the scaling relationships between the size of networks and that of the sub-webs of which they are composed could also be extended to non-natural systems ( e.g. financial44 , transport45 or disease vector dispersal46 networks ) . This would make it possible to verify whether ( i ) systemic risk increases with network size or ( ii ) the rules governing such systems mean that an increase in size is accompanied by increased potential to buffer disturbance , as observed in the food webs analysed in this study . <p> In conclusion , we show that increasing species richness and foraging constraints on food web complexity limit the proportion of species that share food chains in ecosystems . This pattern has not been noticed before . It reduces the intrinsic vulnerability of biodiverse ecological communities to disturbance propagation , and promotes the emergence of species-rich food webs where species organise into effective disturbance-buffering structures in accordance with predictable rules . It is also consistent with the predictions of theoretical research , which highlight the positive effect of adaptive trophic behaviour by consumers on the stability of model food web networks9 . Conversely , the observed results imply that species-poor ecosystems could be highly vulnerable to the propagation of disturbance along food chains , including bottom-up disturbance associated with climate change31,42 , with increased risks for the stability of food webs and the ecosystem services they support47,48,49 . While this study focused on detritus-based food webs , the observed results may be extended to more complete food webs including primary producer-based food chains . Indeed , detrital and herbivore energy pathways are closely interconnected8 , and our observations are consistent with webs generated using the niche model , which was developed and tested against whole food web structures in both aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems6 . Notably , our food web analysis provides mechanism-based evidence indicating that efforts devoted to biodiversity conservation also increase the potential of natural communities to buffer disturbance in ecosystems by maintaining biodiverse , relatively less complex , and ' safer ' food web structures for their constituent species . <h> Materials and Methods <p> We compared habitat-scale detritus-based food webs ( Table 1 ) , reconstructed using population abundance data , carbon and nitrogen stable isotope values and Bayesian isotopic mixing models ( for details on stable isotope analyses and food web reconstruction methods , see Rossi et al.32 and Calizza et al.12,36 ) . Specifically , the habitat-scale food webs were based on taxa and trophic links obtained by sampling multiple patches within each habitat . This made it possible to taking into account intra-habitat variability of occurrence data and the trophic preferences of the various taxa12 . The food webs were representative of six different habitats : a river flowing from a semi-natural to an anthropic landscape ( the River Sacco , referred to as Stream ) , a lowland high-order river embedded in an urban landscape crossing the city of Rome ( the River Tiber , referred to as River ) , a meso-oligotrophic lake ( Lake Bracciano , referred to as Lake ) ; a transitional water system ( the Santa Gilla lagoon , referred to as Lagoon ) , arable land ( referred to as Corn Field ) and a woodland ( referred to as Beech Forest ) ( Table 1 ) . The lower stretches of the two river courses were more heavily anthropised and barriers were present in both cases ( e.g. the city of Rome along the River Tiber ) . Therefore , River and Stream were each divided into upstream and downstream habitats . In all habitats , basal resources were represented by habitat-specific leaf litter colonised by various species of microfungi26,50 . Detailed descriptions of sampling activities and habitats can be found in Rossi et al.32 ( Lake , Lagoon , Beech Forest , Corn Field ) , in Calizza et al.12,36 ( River ) , and in Bentivoglio et al.51 ( Stream ) . <p> Web topology was analysed by determining ( 1 ) species richness , S ; ( 2 ) the number of feeding links , L ; ( 3 ) linkage density , L/S ; ( 4 ) connectance ( Cmin ) as L/S2 ; and ( 5 ) the proportions of total species in the food web accounted for by basal ( %B ) , intermediate ( %I ) and top ( %T ) species . %I was considered to be a measure of prey availability for predators32,36 . The intrinsic vulnerability of food webs to bottom-up , cross and top-down propagation of disturbance ( i.e. starting from basal , intermediate and top species ) was quantified as the proportion of the total number of species ( P ) occurring in each source ( PB ) , cross ( PC ) and sink ( PT ) sub-web respectively24 ( Fig. 1 ) , as follows : <p> $$rmP= ( mathopsum limitsi=1nxpi ) /nx$$ <p> where nx is the number of basal , intermediate and top species used to calculate PB , PC and PT respectively , pi ? = ? Si/ ( S-Ni ) , Si ? = ? the number of species included in the sub-web originating from the ith species , S ? = ? the total number of species in the food web , and Ni ? = ? number of species on the same trophic level as the ith species . The overall vulnerability of the food web to disturbance propagation along food chains ( V ) was measured as the mean P value of all species in the food web . <p> For each parameter , pairwise ratios between habitats were calculated and a matrix containing pairwise comparisons was created . Pairwise values ( n ? = ? 28 ) were plotted and used for correlation models52,53 . A permutation test ( 9999 permutations ) was also run on correlation coefficients , and the observed correlations were considered significant only if robust to permutation ( i.e. with a permutation-based p value ? &lt; ? 0.05 ) . Differences in correlation slopes were tested by analysis of covariance ( ANCOVA ) and the associated homogeneity of slopes test . <p> Based on the observed S and Cmin values , for each habitat , 20 model food webs were generated . Specifically , 10 model food webs were generated based on the niche model6 , a simple yet predictive one-dimensional model able to reproduce the topological properties of real food webs starting from a small number of rules governing the probability of feeding interaction between species . The other 10 model food webs were generated by assigning links between species at random . The PB , PC , PT and V values were calculated and compared with the values measured in the real food webs . In addition , the L and Cmin values expected in accordance with the link-species scaling law33 ( LLSSL , CminLSSL ) and the constant connectance hypothesis34 ( LCCH , CminCCH ) were calculated with reference to the observed S value for each habitat . Using the correlation coefficients obtained from real webs , the PB , PC and PT values were then extrapolated from the correlation with either CminLSSL or CminCCH and compared with the observed data . Food web analysis and modelling were performed with FoodWeb3D software . <h> Acknowledgements <p> This research was supported by PNRA ( PNRA2015/AZ1.01-M.L . @@82767231 <h> The man who lived <p> Warning : This story contains graphic images and descriptions that some readers may find disturbing . <h> I <p> Angel Perez could n't stand the smell . It was fetid , rotten . <p> And it was coming from him . <p> It was July 2018 , and Perez lay helpless in his hospital bed at Cooper University Hospital in Camden . Tubes and wires were draped across his chest , as machines and monitors provided a ceaseless chorus of beeps and hums . <p> His arms and legs had turned gangrenous , a side effect of the drugs keeping him alive after deadly bacteria seeped into his flesh two weeks earlier . The Millville man had been wading in a tributary of the Maurice River near the Delaware Bay when a scratch on his ankle allowed the pathogen inside . <p> " He 's going to die , " said one doctor , hovering over Perez in his hospital bed . <p> Perez heard the comment , but was too weak to respond or protest or beg for an explanation . <p> Angel in his hospital bed at Cooper University Hospital in Camden . His hands and feet were rotting as his body fought a bacterial infection . <p> What was happening was a perfect storm of medical crises : The infection he contracted -- from Vibrio vulnificus , sometimes termed " flesh-eating bacteria " -- had sent him into septic shock , leading to kidney failure . His other organs were also at risk of shutting down . <p> Yet the potent drugs doctors were using to keep his organs alive were simultaneously killing his limbs , starving them of blood supply , causing them to wither and blacken and decompose . <p> Perez would frequently stare at his blackened hands in horror , compulsively peeling off chunks of flaky skin like paint chips off a wall . <p> " Do n't let them take my hands ! " he cried out to his daughter . <p> Doctors were baffled . Infections from V. vulnificus are among the rarest a person can contract . Before 2017 , the hospital had n't seen a case in nearly a decade . But that year brought three cases to Cooper , and Perez would be the first of two there in 2018 . All but one patient contracted the bacterial infection from the same waters of the Delaware Bay , where V. vulnificus would n't be expected to thrive . <p> Dr. Katherine Doktor , an infectious disease specialist on the team treating Perez , remembered her reaction as , " Oh wow , another case . " For Doktor and her colleagues , Perez 's arrival sparked concern of a surge in cases , something seemingly unheard of so far north along the East Coast . Were warming waters caused by climate change creating new opportunities for a deadly pathogen ? <p> For Perez 's wife , daughter and extended family , the confusion was compounded : How could an ordinary day spent crabbing go so horribly wrong ? How could the waters they had visited for years incubate something now killing the man they loved ? <p> " There was so many days when I walked in , and I had nurses coming up to me , telling me , ' Just put him on morphine . Just let him go . ' Doctors telling me , ' Just let him go , ' " recalled Perez 's daughter , Dilena Perez-Dilan . <p> But Angel Perez was n't about to go down without a fight . <h> II <p> Journey down Route 55 out of Vineland , all the way to the southern edge of New Jersey in Cumberland County , and eventually , you 'll come to Matts Landing in Maurice River Township . An idyllic sprawl of pristine and undisturbed marshlands and tributaries , it 's here where the fresh water of the Maurice River ( pronounced Morris , like the county ) meets the salty water of the Delaware Bay . Commercial fishing vessels dock at the few nearby marinas , a small marker of the bustling history of these waters , once known as the oyster capital of the world . <p> Matts Landing in Maurice River Township runs along the marshlands and tributaries of the Maurice River , which feeds into Delaware Bay . It was near this idyllic spot that Angel contracted the bacterial infection that threatened his life . <p> Angel Perez arrived here with his family just after dawn on July 2 , 2018 , the temperature already on its way into the upper 80s . The group -- which included his wife , Haydee , and her cousin and aunt -- set up beside the water and unpacked its gear : crab nets , traps and buckets . Angel tossed in a line as he waded shin-deep into the waters . <p> For Angel , a short , stocky man with the rugged , round face and square jaw of a boxer , this was more than a mere pastime . It was a way for him to recall better days , before his diagnosis of Parkinson 's disease , when his body was entirely his own . Born in the small , mountainous town of Barranquitas , Puerto Rico , he always had been a tactile person , good with his hands . As a kid , he became fascinated with cars and engines and soon began fixing them alongside his neighbor . His ambition was to run his own repair shop when he got older . <p> " That was my fantasy , " he recalled decades later . <p> He moved to New Jersey by himself at 16 to help his older sister during her pregnancy . In 1989 , he had a daughter , Dilena Perez-Dilan , though his relationship with her mother did n't last . In the late 1990s , he met and married Haydee . And for two decades , Angel got to live his modest dream , operating a small used car dealership and auto body shop in Millville . <p> Angel and Haydee on their wedding day in the late 1990s . He lived his dream for 15 years -- owning a used car dealership and auto body shop . <p> Today , all that 's left of the business can be found in his backyard , where more than 40 unsold vehicles -- rusted Hondas , Nissans and Toyotas -- sit idly behind his home , arranged in neat rows and at haphazard angles like dusty trophies from the old days . <p> In 2004 , Angel 's body started betraying him : unexplained tremors , spasms , stiffness in his muscles . He was diagnosed with Parkinson 's a year later . The physical toll of mechanical work soon became too much to bear , and he shuttered the shop . <p> By 2018 , he had trouble walking and driving . His once-confident speech sounded halting and gravelly . <p> He turned to his faith around the time of his diagnosis , attending Temple of Faith Church in Vineland two , even three times a week with Haydee . He trusted God had a plan that would see him through his physical decline . <p> His other refuge was the bay , crabbing the waters along Matts Landing . On a calm day , the only real sound comes from the chirping shorebirds perched in a line of trees across the way . The setting brought him a sense of spiritual and physical peace . The water loosened his muscles and calmed his tremors and spasms . <p> Angel , right , and his wife 's cousin crabbing near the Delaware Bay . The waters that flow into the bay were Angel 's sanctuary after he was diagnosed with Parkinson 's disease . <p> If only for a few hours , he felt like the person he once was . <p> " It was like his sanctuary , " his daughter said . <p> The morning of July 2 , 2018 , felt particularly satisfying . <p> Angel 's trips to the water had grown infrequent over the years . But Haydee said she 'd bring him on a few outings that week . Christian music played on a speaker they 'd brought , as the four laughed and joked and took turns tossing in throw lines . Angel proudly held up his net full of crabs to show everyone knew who was boss of those waters . Haydee , who has jet black hair , olive skin and a shy , reserved manner , held up a crab of her own , one that was as big as her face , before tossing it in one of the buckets with the rest . <p> Angel did n't know it yet , but it would be the last time he would ever feel the water wash over his fingers and feet . <h> III <p> Under a microscope , it looks almost like a computer mouse -- a curved rod with a squiggly tail protruding from one end . <p> It thrives in warm , brackish waters , where it incubates and multiplies . It can enter through an open wound , as it did with Angel , or through the consumption of raw or undercooked shellfish . While it works its way through the body , it can evade the immune system and offer few clues to its presence , other than perhaps a few benign-looking symptoms such as redness and swelling on the skin . <p> V. vulnificus , as it 's medically known , is one of about 100 Vibrio species -- roughly a dozen of which can cause illness -- and is part of the same family as cholera . It is usually harmless to people with a healthy immune system . Some may experience only mild symptoms akin to food poisoning before the body naturally eradicates the bacteria . <p> But for others , especially those who are immunocompromised , there are risks of life-threatening complications . In rare cases , when V. vulnificus enters through a scratch or cut , toxins released by the microbes can cause the wound to develop necrotizing fasciitis , an illness more commonly known as " flesh-eating disease , " which corrodes and kills soft tissue and can spread throughout the entire surface of the body . <p> In those instances , it is n't necessarily " flesh-eating disease " that ends up killing patients . Instead , sepsis -- a blood infection that can occur when the body is attempting to fend off serious infection -- often causes a drastic drop in blood pressure and leads to multiple organ failure . <p> On the evening of July 2 , 2018 , Haydee cooked a batch of crabs they 'd caught that morning . The couple , married for 21 years , then enjoyed a quiet evening together . <p> Nothing seemed out of the ordinary . <p> The first signs of trouble arrived the next morning , when Angel noticed his right ankle was red and swollen . He did n't think much of it at first , but decided to get it checked at a nearby urgent care center . A doctor there said it looked like cellulitis , a common bacterial skin infection . He prescribed antibiotics , which Angel filled on the way home . <p> But the pain creeping up his leg was getting worse . The soreness grew into a burning , stabbing pain in his ankle . <p> This small scratch on Angel 's right ankle marks the beginning of his ordeal . Rare bacteria seeped into the scrape and caused a perfect storm of medical crises . <p> " It felt like my leg was going to burst , " Angel recalled . <p> Seeing her usually composed husband near tears , Haydee called an ambulance , which rushed him to an emergency room in Vineland , the next town over . But again , the doctor he saw there was n't especially alarmed . <p> Continue with the antibiotics , he told Angel , and come back if it gets worse . <p> That night , Angel 's leg swelled so much it looked like a fleshy tube with no ankle . Blisters were forming on the skin . <p> Haydee rushed him to the emergency room , this time in Elmer , in neighboring Salem County . But doctors still had few answers . Even though V. vulnificus infections are covered in medical textbooks , they are not something most clinicians are accustomed to seeing in New Jersey . <p> " It was always a Florida sort of infection , " said Dr. David Cennimo , an infectious disease expert at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School . <p> But for clinicians in New Jersey , he said : " This is one of the things that you now have to think about . " <p> In the examination room at the hospital , Angel could barely speak from the pain . Doctors started him on broad-spectrum antibiotics , which are used when the source of a bacterial infection is unknown . An operation to drain the leg of rapidly building fluid would be essential . <p> Cooper University Hospital was the fourth and final medical facility that treated Angel . <p> In the early morning of July 4 , 2018 , Angel was rushed by ambulance to Cooper University Hospital , his fourth and final medical facility in 24 hours . His blood pressure and oxygen levels were dropping . A breathing tube was inserted down his throat as his lungs struggled for air . He was placed into a coma and wheeled into the operating room . <p> That first procedure , called a fasciotomy and done in the hopes of salvaging the rapidly deteriorating leg , was just the start of Angel 's odyssey . Cultures soon would explain what was happening inside his body . <p> The diagnosis : V. vulnificus infection , complicated by sepsis and flesh-eating disease on his leg . <p> The death rate for such patients ? <p> More than 50% . <h> IV <p> Every medical story is , in effect , a mystery . <p> Doctors play the role of detective -- asking questions , considering test results , eliminating possibilities -- until arriving at a diagnosis . In the case of a possible epidemic , there are other mysteries : How was the illness contracted ? Who might be susceptible ? How can it be stopped before it infects others ? <p> For much of the previous year before she encountered Angel Perez , Doktor , the infectious diseases specialist at Cooper University Hospital , was wrestling with a mystery : Why had three cases of V. vulnificus infection turned up in her South Jersey hospital ? <p> " Why now ? " Doktor remembered asking herself . <p> Vibrio vulnificus , sometimes called " flesh-eating bacteria , " is part of the same family as cholera . It is usually harmless to people with a healthy immune system . But some face life-threatening complications . <p> Such infections are rare to begin with -- only about 200 cases are reported in the U.S. each year , according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . Most occur in states near the warm waters of the Southeastern U.S. and Gulf Coast . Until recently , V. vulnificus infections were almost nonexistent in New Jersey . <p> The first case Cooper saw came in July 2017 , when a 38-year-old man presented at the hospital with V. vulnificus in his bloodstream and flesh-eating disease on his left calf . How the man contracted the bacterial infection , though , was never clearly established : He told specialists he worked at a seafood restaurant , but insisted he had n't been crabbing or fishing before he got sick . The man survived . <p> Dr. Katherine Doktor , an infectious disease specialist on the Cooper University Hospital team treating Angel , was surprised to see so many V. vulnificus-related infections in her hospital . <p> Two more cases arrived at Cooper in September 2017 , just weeks apart . A 64-year-old man died in the hospital from an infection he contracted after crabbing in the Delaware Bay . And a 46-year-old man was admitted with an infection and flesh-eating disease after cutting his left leg while crabbing in the same area . ( He survived . ) <p> By the time Angel arrived the following July with an eerily similar story -- a day crabbing in waters that fed the Delaware Bay and with a cut on his leg -- the connection was unavoidable . <p> " We were questioning , ' Is this ( area ) now a habitat for them ? ' " said Doktor , who has auburn-brown hair , a soft voice and a notable sense of humor about her last name . " Before , the cool temperature of the water was not very hospitable for their growth . So was the Delaware Bay becoming warmer and now making a new home for the bacteria to grow ? " <p> It 's one of the least considered aspects of climate change -- that a warming planet and rising sea temperatures can lead to the spread of deadly bacteria . <p> But that 's what appears to be happening , according to experts . <p> " The Delaware Bay has been free of infections -- maybe once in a decade or something -- but it 's changing , " said Rita Colwell , professor at the University of Maryland at College Park and Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg School of Public Health . <p> " In my opinion , yes , something definitely is happening , " she added . <p> Some researchers see the bacteria 's changing behavior as a " barometer of climate change " -- an early warning sign for the years ahead , said Craig Baker-Austin , senior research scientist and director of the UK National Reference Laboratory . <p> " Very few human pathogens have that kind of relationship with the environment , " Baker-Austin said . <p> Infections from V. vulnificus bacteria have been rare in New Jersey waters . But that seems to be changing due to climate change . <p> V. vulnificus flourishes in the warm , salty water found in bays and estuaries , which also provide just enough fresh water for the bacteria to grow . First isolated and identified in 1976 , V. vulnificus always has been present in the Delaware Bay . But , historically , New Jersey never had to worry . The cooler waters surrounding the state had never been suitable enough for the bacteria to pose a threat . <p> That appears to be changing . According to Baker-Austin , V. vulnificus and other Vibrio species have been detected in the ice-cold waters of the Baltic Sea , and infections from the bacteria have emerged in Denmark , Finland and Sweden . <p> In New Jersey , air temperatures have risen 2 degrees Celsius over the past 125 years , the third-highest increase in the nation , according to an August analysis by The Washington Post . Much of that increase has occurred within the past three decades . <p> The Delaware Bay has warmed 1.2 to 1.9 degrees Celsius over the past 16 years , according to Matt Oliver , the Patricia and Charles Robertson associate professor of marine science and policy at the University of Delaware . <p> Every degree warmer boosts bacteria 's ability to divide and multiply . The increased melting of glaciers is also producing more fresh water in the oceans , allowing bacteria to venture beyond their typical range . <p> " Two degrees is extremely significant , " said Jim Oliver , a professor of microbiology at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte . " It 's going to mean that a lot of places that have never seen this bacteria will now see it . " <h> V <p> In his hospital room at Cooper , Angel Perez and his family knew none of this . <p> The medical mystery of how and why this happened had taken a back seat to an increasingly urgent challenge : keeping Angel alive . <p> A group of a dozen or so friends and family members had settled in to keep vigil , sleeping on the floor , an air mattress and even in chairs in the hospital waiting room . <p> Angel 's pastor and members of his church visited almost daily . With one hand on Angel 's forehead , the other raised in the air , the pastor delivered a prayer as the others followed along , arms raised above their heads , palms tilted to the ceiling . Angel would try to follow along , but his speech was often garbled and slurred . <p> " There were so many people just praying for him ... and just praying for a miracle from God to come upon him , " said the Rev. Israel Delgado of Temple of Faith Church in Vineland . <p> Angel 's arms and legs withered and blackened from gangrene as his doctors fought to stop the infection . He faced a bitter crossroads : lose his hands and feet to amputation or die . <p> The most immediate threat to Angel remained sepsis and his dangerously low blood pressure . To get blood pumping to the heart , brain and other vital organs , doctors administered a potent class of drugs called vasopressors , or pressors . The drugs divert blood from elsewhere in the body -- non-vital organs and the arms and legs -- and rush it to the vital organs . <p> Siphoning blood from the arms and legs , however , puts the appendages at risk of developing gangrene . Doctors hoped the death of tissue would n't go beyond his fingers and toes , where discoloration initially emerged . <p> " You 're having to weigh daily , are the benefits worth the risks ? " said Dr. David Fuller , one of Angel 's primary doctors , who serves as director of upper extremity surgery at Cooper . <p> After the first week , doctors brought the bacteria under control and staved off the flesh-eating infection on his leg . But the gangrene was showing no signs of abating . By the middle of July , it had spread halfway up his forearms and shins . Angel 's rotting limbs almost certainly would become a feeding ground for new bacteria and further infection . The only option would be amputation . Yet his doctors did n't believe he was strong enough to survive surgery . <p> At the center of all this , attempting to serve as her father 's advocate and her family 's spokeswoman , was Dilena Perez-Dilan , Angel 's daughter . ( While Haydee was supportive of the reporting of this story , she said she was shy and did n't want to discuss Angel 's plight at length . Both Angel and Dilena later speculated that talking about it was simply too upsetting for Haydee . ) <p> Standing 5 feet , 4 inches , with olive skin and dark brown hair , Dilena was regularly talking to doctors after Haydee had designated her as their point person . She had taken leave from her job as a social worker and had n't slept at her home in New Castle , Delaware , since her dad was admitted to Cooper . And she had barely seen her 6-year-old son . <p> Dilena always had been close to her father . She saw him as stoic and strong . As a child , she rarely saw him cry . <p> Dilena Perez-Dilan serves as her father 's advocate and the family spokeswoman as his story made headlines around the world . <p> But now it was Dilena who refused to cry in front of her father . <p> " He felt what was going on , and I did n't want to show him ( my tears ) , " she said . <p> The situation was growing dire . His hallucinations were becoming more intense -- delusions of men trying to break into his room and kill him . <p> He 'd scream at the top of his lungs : " Hallelujah ! Hallelujah ! " <p> Dilena recalled a day in the hospital when she was just staring at her father 's arms and legs , almost awed by the grotesque transformation . <p> " The color was just black , " she said . And the smell pervaded his room . <p> " The closer you got to it , the more powerful the smell was , " she said . <p> Near the end of July , according to Dilena , the care team told the family her father still was n't strong enough for surgery . But unless his limbs were removed , he would have a little more than a week to live -- days of continued anguish and decline . <p> Angel began summoning family into his room around this time , telling everyone he loved them and basically " giving a verbal will to everybody , " Dilena said . <p> " He was making amends with people . He brought me in and told me everything he wanted to tell me , " she said . <p> He told Dilena to take care of her son and to buy a home . <p> " He talked about how proud he was of me and that he was grateful to have me as his daughter and that he tried his best with me , " she said . <p> Around Aug. 1 , the family consented to put Angel in hospice in another wing of the hospital -- though staff had called it " comfort care . " With all the information being hurled at them , Dilena and Haydee did n't fully understand treatment would cease , except for the slow drip of morphine to dull the pain until Angel 's body gave out altogether . <p> Not long after settling in the new room , Dilena and Haydee panicked . Had they made a terrible decision ? Within an hour , the pair went to Angel 's bedside to explain exactly where he was . <p> He had been slipping in and out of delirium for weeks . But at that moment , Angel gazed up and in his frail , fragile voice said he wanted to resume treatment . <p> " We went to my dad -- me and my stepmom -- and we said , ' Dad , what do you want to do ? What do you think you can handle ? ' " Dilena recalled . <p> " He was like , ' No , I want to fight . I want to keep fighting . ' So , once he said he was going to keep fighting , we got up , we walked over and we told the lead nurse . ... ' We no longer want to be on this comfort care . My dad does n't want to do this . He wants to be treated . ' " <p> All told , Angel spent four hours in hospice care . <h> VI <p> In medicine , talk of miracles is often discouraged . It can raise false hope in dire circumstances , and it minimizes the hard , practical work doctors do to combat illness . <p> There 's a reason , though , the word endures in medical conversations . In many recoveries , doctors ca n't entirely explain why some recover and others do n't . <p> Dr. David Fuller , director of upper extremity surgery at Cooper University Hospital , was one of Angel 's primary doctors . <p> When Dr. David Fuller , who is tall , thin and has gray hair , first met Angel , he did not think the patient would survive . But then , " He started getting a little stronger . His blood pressure , heart rate -- things started becoming more stable , and he was requiring less and less pressors , " Fuller said . " And I think that 's what really turned the tide in his recovery . " <p> Ultimately , even Fuller was surprised by Angel 's turnaround . <p> " What was it that allowed him to survive ? I do n't think any of us can answer that question , " Fuller said . <p> The gangrene seemed to have run its course , stopping 5 or 6 inches below both kneecaps and a few inches below Angel 's elbows , with a gruesome line on the flesh showing the separation of the dead , black tissue and healthy tissue . The split , known medically as the " line of demarcation , " is something the body produces on its own , signaling to surgeons where they should amputate a gangrenous limb . <p> A week after Angel left hospice , doctors told him they would have to amputate his limbs . The surgery to remove both forearms was scheduled for Aug. 8 . Fuller explained the risks to Angel and his family . He told them there was still a chance Angel would die during surgery . <p> And then Fuller presented Angel and his family with a consent form . <p> Angel did nothing . <p> He would n't speak or answer the doctor . He would n't give consent . The family was hesitant to sign on his behalf , believing it was his call . <p> " We did n't want to make a decision without him saying yes or no , " Dilena said . <p> The surgery was scrapped . <p> Several days passed in uncertainty . Fuller tried to emphasize to Angel the significance of the opportunity . Dilena pleaded as well . For the first time , her exhaustion and worry spilled over into frustration . <p> Angel 's hands could not be saved . When he knocked them together , they made a haunting sound " like two rocks banging together . " <p> " I told him , ' Dad , you need to let us know what you want to do , because when the time came for us to make the decision and give our word , we asked you , and you did n't respond , ' " she recalled saying to him . <p> She later added , " I think he was very scared . " <p> Then one night , Dilena recalled , her father knocked his hands against each other . They made a gruesome sound . <p> " ( It was ) like two rocks banging together because they were so , so dried out , " she said . <p> For weeks , Angel 's family and friends had known there would be no saving his limbs . But Angel kept believing otherwise , that somehow they might be regenerated , the way a spider can regrow its legs . <p> " Do what you got ta do , " Angel told the doctors , finally consenting to surgery . <p> The first surgery took place on Aug. 15 . An anesthetized Angel lay flat under the beaming LED surgical lights , eyes closed , a breathing tube down his throat . Fuller and the team went to work , carefully amputating his arms a few inches below the elbows . After the limbs were removed , skin flaps were sown . His nubs were wrapped , and he was moved to recovery . <p> The entire procedure took roughly six hours . But it was only half the battle -- a second surgery to amputate his legs would still need to be scheduled . <p> Angel remembers little from the hours and days that followed . He was groggy and disoriented from the anesthesia . His flickering nerves were still telling his brain his hands were there . <p> For her part , Dilena became obsessed with the idea she had to get her dad outside , if only to the hospital courtyard , before his next surgery . He had been living inside a hospital room for weeks . She believed she owed him a breath of fresh air . <p> The hospital would n't authorize it because of the risk of further infection , but a nurse the family befriended said she 'd help . Before dawn on a late August morning , the nurse and Dilena hoisted Angel into a wheelchair , hurried him down the hallway , past security and out to the courtyard , where a garden and gravel paths encircle a stone tile waterfall . <p> The sun had n't come up . Dilena recalled the crisp dawn air , the chirping birds . Her father would have his legs amputated soon . But at that moment , all concerns faded . <p> When the sun began to rise , they both started to cry . After nearly two months , this would be the moment Dilena finally let her father see her tears . <p> " He just stared at the sky , " she said . " At one point , he fell asleep because it was so early , and then he would wake back up , and his eyes got big . " <p> About a week and a half later , Angel underwent his next surgery . Both of his legs were removed a few inches below the kneecaps . <h> VII <p> There 's a playbook for most illnesses , dreadful but familiar . No one wants to watch a loved one fight cancer or recover from a stroke . But there is comfort , at least , in our understanding of the contours of those battles . We know what triumph over such illnesses looks like , just as we have learned to recognize the warning signs of likely defeat . <p> But what happened to Angel Perez was of a different order entirely . Few of us know what flesh-eating disease looks like , much less how you go about recovering from it . <p> And the psychic toll would seem to be incomprehensible : to be out crabbing one day , and then to learn , just a short time later , that your arms and legs must be amputated if there is any hope of surviving ? <p> I learned about Angel Perez on July 8 , 2018 , just a few days after he arrived at Cooper University Hospital , when word of his medical crisis made its way to the NJ Advance Media newsroom . I interviewed Dilena by telephone the next day , and she spoke of both the randomness of her father 's plight and his faith and his determination in the face of the unimaginable . <p> " He 's been praising God nonstop , " Dilena told me during that first call . " He 's just happy to have a second chance . " <p> Angel 's daily physical therapy routine included exercises such as hitting and catching balloons to teach him how to use what remains of his limbs . <p> I reported on the story throughout the summer of 2018 , as Angel 's condition worsened , and news of his plight made national and international headlines . When he somehow survived the ordeal , the media attention naturally faded . But a new set of challenges and agonies presented themselves . <p> Would faith and family be enough to carry Angel through the long recovery ahead ? <p> How do you rebuild a life without limbs , especially if you 're a man whose livelihood once depended on your hands ? <p> Dilena invited me to meet her father in late September last year , just after he had been discharged and moved to a rehabilitation facility in Vineland . Back in July , she sent me a photo of Angel , which we published with our stories . In that photo , he 's wearing a black baseball cap crooked and low on his head and holding out a crabbing net to the camera , with several crabs at the bottom . Although the net obscures his face , you can see his grin , perhaps prideful , perhaps mischievous , maybe both . <p> But now , as I stepped into his room , I saw a different man entirely . A frail-looking Angel sat in a wheelchair , wearing black athletic shorts and a teal T-shirt . His arms were amputated below the elbow . His right leg was amputated almost entirely up to his kneecap . His left leg was amputated about 4 or 5 inches lower . <p> Despite his faith and the considerable progress he has made , Angel battles despair , thinking about all he has lost . <p> His face was pale and gaunt , his torso a mere shell . His daughter said he lost 40 pounds while in the hospital before the amputations . Thick , raised scar tissue branched in different directions on the nub of his left arm like the roots of a tree . <p> Dilena was there that day , and so was Angel 's older sister , Aida Perez . She was one of four sisters , but the one who always looked after him when they were kids . Together , we watched as he went about his daily physical therapy routine , exercises designed to teach him to use what remained of his limbs . That day , he was learning to roll over on a bed , posting his nubs on the surface and then rotating his torso . He ping-ponged a balloon back and forth with one therapist , hitting it with the right nub , then with the left . She then had him clamp the balloon with both nubs to get used to grabbing objects without his hands . <p> As a pair of physical therapists hoisted her father from his wheelchair and onto the bed , Dilena began to cry . Aida stood by the wall , looking on quietly . The therapists stretched Angel 's muscles , pushing down on his kneecaps . Just below the right nub was a thick line from the surgical incision that had been made about a month earlier . You could see the fading marks from the sutures that kept the folded skin flaps sewn together , not unlike the seams of a baseball . <p> Angel struggles to operate a TV remote control , one of the everyday challenges he faces after the amputation of his four limbs . <p> Angel signaled that he was fine and not in pain . He 'd been having trouble speaking since arriving at the rehab facility . When he did , he was barely audible . <p> The physical therapists secured him through his armpits and shifted his body toward the head of the bed , positioning him upright for the next exercise . To me , Angel looked utterly helpless . The therapists then showed him how to put on and take off his T-shirt -- one therapist recommended he bite down on the neckline to keep it steady as he slipped his limbs in and out of the sleeves . <p> Yet despite the obvious anguish of the session , Angel seemed hopeful , almost unaffected as I asked him questions . <p> He was adamant he had never felt fear . <p> " The doctors had more fear than I had , " he mumbled . <p> Everything had been in God 's hands , he said . Everything was still in God 's hands . <p> Dilena interjected , reminding him of the grim moments she 'd witnessed , about the anguish he felt before the amputations . <p> " I was there with you , " she said to her father . <p> Angel said he did n't question God 's plan . <p> He had always taken pains to be the stable , competent man he believed a father should be while raising his daughter , according to Dilena . He always shielded his daughter from seeing him vulnerable . She rarely saw him emotional . She never even saw him argue with Haydee -- or anyone for that matter . <p> " He never showed me any of that , " she said . <p> On that September afternoon , I saw a man doing the same , struggling between stoicism and vulnerability , still trying to protect his daughter , even as he needed help going to the bathroom or feeding himself . <p> " It was God 's will , " Angel said to me , tacks in the shape of a cross pinned to a board behind him . <h> VIII <p> On a frigid day this February , I traveled with another journalist and Angel , his daughter and his sister Aida to the same waters he had been crabbing seven months earlier . We parked along the narrow dirt road of Matts Landing , not far from the tributary where Angel had contracted the bacterial infection . I had been hesitant to propose the trip for fear of retraumatizing Angel . But he seemed willing , even eager to go , almost as if he were again determined to prove his fearlessness . <p> Even a trip to the diner presents challenges . Angel uses a wheelchair and must be hoisted into the car for appointments . <p> His daughter helped Angel out of the car and into his wheelchair . She pushed him into the middle of the soggy , single-lane road , surrounded by the marshy tributaries . There was no one else in sight . Angel looked out at the water where , presumably , bacteria were hibernating , which occurs when water temperatures drop below 55 degrees Fahrenheit . <p> For a long time , he was quiet . And then , the sun in his eyes , Angel praised God . <p> " I got my heart and my soul , and I still have my brain , " he said . <p> The journey to this point had been brutal and unrelenting , but Angel was still thankful . Thankful for his life . Thankful for his faith . And thankful for his daughter . <p> Near the end of our trip , he teared up when speaking about her . <p> " She 's the greatest daughter I 've ever had in my life . She -- ever since she was a little girl -- she was gon na care for her daddy , " he said . <p> Back home that afternoon , Angel proudly showed me the headway he had been making in his recovery , mastering the use of his wheelchair and learning to utilize his limbs . Paddling the wheels with his forearms , he glided over to the refrigerator and pried open the door . In the bedroom , he climbed onto the bed and clicked the television remote using his elbow . <p> His biggest hope , however , remained out of reach -- walking on prosthetics . Wincing , he showed me the nerve endings that still wiggle on their own beneath the flaps of scar tissue , endlessly searching to reconnect with the wiring doctors had removed . Those snipped nerves make walking anew challenging for many amputees . <p> A woman at church bandages maracas to Angel 's arm stumps so that he could play along with the choir . <p> When Angel tried to walk on prosthetics , the nerves shot a pain like a zap of electricity whenever he put weight into the sockets . His Parkinson's-related tremors threw him further off balance . <p> " I have hope one day I 'll be walking , " he said . <p> I visited him a few more times over the next few months . Each time , I tried to understand how Angel could remain so calm and stoic in the face of a life so brutally transformed . <p> But it was n't until late May , in his living room , that Angel finally opened up . He was squirming terribly in his wheelchair that afternoon from his Parkinson 's , and you could barely understand him . He was frustrated by his slurred , obstructed speech , often trying to force the words out of his mouth . <p> But tentatively , Angel admitted some days he feels despair instead of hope . Then he finally acknowledged the depths of his despondency during those harrowing two months in the hospital . <p> Angel holds out hope that he will one day walk again with the help of prosthetics . But each day is a struggle , requiring help to do ordinary tasks such as eating . <p> " I was ready to give up , " he said , referring to late July 2018 . <p> He suggested that one of the hardest parts of his recovery had been seeing others just go about their regular business . He told me about the hours and hours he spent sitting in the living room , staring out the window , watching cars pass and people walk by . He would wonder where they were headed while he remained stuck as if tied to a chair with rope . <p> " I have no legs . I do n't have any arms . What am I here for ? " he said he would sometimes wonder . <p> He wondered , too , whether anything could have been done to save his limbs : What if those first doctors had diagnosed him earlier and started proper antibiotic treatment right away ? What if he had n't needed such a high dose of pressors ? <p> Still , he said , the worst was behind him -- the despair had lasted about six months after he returned home . Now he was able to start enjoying life again . And even though his prosthetic legs rested in the corner of a room like one of the cars in his backyard , he was determined that one day he would walk again . <p> " I have n't finished my journey , " he said . <h> IX <p> In September 2018 , a 64-year-old man who cut his leg using a crab trap while in the Delaware Bay contracted a V. vulnificus infection -- the fifth case Cooper University Hospital would see in two years . ( He survived after going into shock , developing blisters on his body and ultimately needing extensive tissue removed . ) According to the New Jersey Department of Health , a sixth infection also happened last year , though the state did not release details or say which hospital treated the patient . <p> In June 2019 , the Annals of Internal Medicine published a paper co-authored by Dr. Katherine Doktor , outlining the five cases that had appeared at Cooper and warning that " non-endemic areas may start to see an increase in V. vulnificus related infections " because of rising sea temperatures . <p> Later in the year , six additional people in New Jersey were diagnosed with V. vulnificus infections , according to the New Jersey Department of Health . <p> For his part , Angel , who has regained some of the weight he lost in the hospital , gets around these days with the help of a motorized wheelchair . He will never feel the water again with his hands and feet , but he still longs to go crabbing again at Matts Landing with his daughter and wife . <p> Dilena Perez-Dilan , Angel 's daughter , was with him throughout his hospital stay and recovery . <p> And he still wants to walk , though as of December , Angel still has not taken a step . He relies on Medicaid -- which has covered his medical bills , the family said -- and the cost of new prosthetics is prohibitive . <p> Still , Dr. David Fuller , who still sees Angel once every three months , has n't entirely ruled out the possibility . <p> " The story is not done , and this is week to week , and month to month , " Fuller said . <p> Of my many visits with Angel over the past 15 months , one stands out . It was July 2 , 2019 , exactly a year after his fateful crabbing trip , a blazing hot day when the temperature climbed into the low 90s . The sun filtered through the windows into the house that afternoon , brightening the rooms . Haydee , who had watched her husband teeter on the brink of death for weeks , was there . As she had during previous visits , she kept her distance , but helped gather medical records , photos , videos and other materials for me . <p> " The past is the past , " she said in the living room , shuffling through papers and files -- her final words to me on what happened to her husband . <p> Later , at the dining room table , she was scrolling through what appeared to be hundreds of photos and videos she had taken while Angel was in the hospital , most of which he does n't remember ever being taken . <p> As Haydee scrolled and scrolled on the laptop , Angel , now 61 , just sat quietly , watching himself in those videos and images as if looking at a stranger . I then showed him the trailer of a short documentary that our videographer had put together , using much of the family 's footage . <p> Angel 's eyes were glued to the video that showed him in his hospital bed . He stared and said nothing . <p> With his arms and legs still attached to his body , he saw the person he once was -- his past . <p> In the next room , a pair of prosthetics rested unused in the corner against a wall -- Angel 's future . <p> Angel admitted some days he feels despair instead of hope . <p> Enter your email address to receive updates about this project and future investigations :

" <p> Buttigieg was asked about Trump 's record on the press . <p> " He is echoing vocabulary of dictators around the world , " Buttigieg said . " When the American president refers to unfavorable press coverage as the product of the enemy of the people , Democracy around the world gets weaker . " <h> Buttigieg defends climate record <p> Update : 8:40 p.m . <p> Buttigieg said climate change will be a first-day action , responding to some criticism by Steyer . The mayor said he proposes a carbon tax and investment in renewable energy . <p> Buttigieg said he lives along the river in South Bend and so has seen first-hand how historic floods have caused damage . It 's a point he often makes on the campaign trail , in which he points out South Bend has had two historic floods since he has been mayor . <p> He also said politicians need to engage everyday people , like auto workers and farmers , in solutions rather than " beat them over the head " with policy changes . <h> Buttigieg says progressives present a false choice <p> Update : 8:35 p.m . <p> Buttigieg indicated that Americans are being offered a false choice by certain progressive ideas . <p> When asked about Warren 's spending proposals on items such as Medicare for All , Buttigieg said it seems that " we either have to go all the way to the extreme or it 's business as usual . " <p> He said taxes on the rich and corporations would have to go up , but he said it can be done without spending the amount of money that economists say will hurt the economy . <p> He referenced his plan to have free tuition for college for all but the top 20 percent of wage earners . <p> " On issue after issue we have got to break out of the Washington mindset that measures the bigness of an idea by how many trillions of dollars it adds to the budget or the boldness of an idea by how many fellow Americans it can antagonize , " he said . <h> Buttigieg says lagging wages are the result of bad policies <p> Update : 8:25 p.m . <p> Buttigieg said that while the stock market is soaring , regular people doing bills at the end of the month are finding their wages are n't keeping up with the rising costs of owning a house and health care . <p> " Where I live , folks are n't measuring the economy by how the Dow Jones is doing , " he said . " They are measuring the economy by how they are doing . " <p> He said it 's also important to understand that the working poor are struggling . <p> He said there is n't one county in the country where someone working full time at the minimum wage can afford a two-bedroom apartment . Most places , he said , they ca n't afford a one-bedroom apartment . <p> " The biggest problem in our economy is simple , " he said . " People are not getting paid enough . That is not the result of some mysterious cosmic force . It is the result of bad policies , and we have got to change it by raising wages and empowering workers . " <p> It 's not all good news , though , for the mayor of South Bend . He still has ground to make up among black and Latino voters as evidenced by his lagging status in South Carolina , the first racially diverse state to hold a nominating contest . <p> Today 's debate , which is scheduled for 8-11 p.m. on PBS and CNN , is his next opportunity to make his case to a wider audience . <p> The debate field has narrowed after the Democratic National Committee raised the fundraising and polling standards to qualify . Also participating will be former Vice President Joe Biden , Sens . Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota , Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts , billionaire Tom Steyer and entrepreneur Andrew Yang .
